title: Data and Research Question
text:
The Youth Risk Behavior Survey (YRBS) is a national survey that monitors health-related behaviors among high school students, including weapon carrying and associated risk factors.



Source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
Year: 2023
Target Population: High school students
Sample Size: Approximately 19,000 students nationwide




How do logistic regression, lasso, k-nearest neighbors, and tree-based models compare in predicting school-based weapon carrying among adolescents based on risk and protective factors?



The dataset includes information on various health-related behaviors:

Outcome

Weapon Carrying (Carried a weapon on school property)

Predictors

Traumatic experiences
School Safety Perceptions
Bullying Experiences
Family Support
Social Media Use
Peer Relationships

And so forth…






library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(here)
data(clean_yrbs_2023)





analysis_data <- clean_yrbs_2023 %>%
    select(
        WeaponCarryingSchool, AttackedInNeighborhood, Bullying,
        SexualAbuseByOlderPerson, ParentalPhysicalAbuse, ParentSubstanceUse,
        ParentIncarceration, SchoolConnectedness, ParentalMonitoring,
        UnfairDisciplineAtSchool, Homelessness
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(WeaponCarryingSchool)) %>%
    mutate(across(
        c(
            ParentSubstanceUse, ParentIncarceration, SchoolConnectedness,
            ParentalMonitoring, UnfairDisciplineAtSchool
        ),
        ~ as.numeric(.x) - 1
    )) %>%
    mutate(across(
        c(
            ParentSubstanceUse, ParentIncarceration, SchoolConnectedness,
            ParentalMonitoring, UnfairDisciplineAtSchool
        ),
        ~ factor(.x)
    ))





set.seed(1990)

analysis_split <- initial_split(analysis_data,
    strata = WeaponCarryingSchool
)

analysis_train <- training(analysis_split)
analysis_test <- testing(analysis_split)

analysis_split





analysis_folds <- vfold_cv(analysis_train,
    v = 5
)
analysis_folds

title: Lasso Regression
text:
Lasso regression is a statistical model that combines linear/logistic regression with L1 regularization to perform both variable selection and regularization. The term “Lasso” stands for “Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator.” This method is particularly useful when dealing with datasets that have many predictors, as it helps to:

Reduce overfitting by penalizing large coefficients
Perform automatic feature selection by shrinking some coefficients to exactly zero
Handle multicollinearity by selecting only one variable from a group of highly correlated predictors

In this analysis, I used Lasso regression to predict weapon carrying behavior in schools, demonstrating how this method can help identify the most important predictors while maintaining model interpretability.

Data Preprocessing
Before fitting the model, I needed to preprocess the data. I created a recipe that:

Imputes missing values in categorical variables using the mode
Imputes missing values in numeric variables using the mean
Removes predictors with zero variance
Removes highly correlated predictors (correlation threshold = 0.7)
Creates dummy variables for categorical predictors


lasso_weapon_carry_recipe <- 
  recipe(formula = WeaponCarryingSchool ~ ., data = analysis_train) |>
  step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
  step_impute_mean(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors()) |> 
  step_corr(all_numeric_predictors(), threshold = 0.7) %>% 
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())

text:
Results and Interpretation
Again, the model fails to be exceptional. In fact, the AUC was slightly smaller than that from my logistic model. Accuracy stayed high at 95.7%, which is expected given the class imbalance. The model is good at predicting who did not carry a weapon but struggles with those who did. However, it’s not all bad. The model was successful in reproducing results on unseen data (re: a Brier score of 0.04), and we see a similar importance of variables as in the logistic model. The consistency with which violence-related variables have the highest impact increases my certainty that these are genuine risk factors.

Results and Interpretation

Model Performance
The logistic regression model was successful, but not great. An AUC (area under the curve) of 0.69 is decent for an ROC curve. It was trained to predict weapon-carrying behavior in schools, showing extremely high sensitivity (0.999) but very low specificity (0.014). This indicates that the model is nearly perfect at identifying students who did not carry weapons, but it struggles to correctly identify students who did.
This imbalance suggests the model errs on the side of over-predicting weapon carrying, which may be desirable in some safety-first scenarios (e.g. school interventions), but limits its overall precision.
This is an example of how simple models (in this case, linear regression) don’t always give the intended results, often oversimplifying. Machine learning can be used to increase the precision of our model later on.


Predictor Effects
Still, there are interesting takeaways re: the impact of certain conditions on a teenagers likelihood to bring a gunt o school. In moments like this, we have to remember the story behind the numbers.
For example, we see variables related to violence massively increase the odds of bringing a gun to school (“AttackedInNeighborhood” and “ParentalPhysicalAbuse” were both in the top three for highest exponentiated logistic regression coefficients.)
Meanwhile, conditions at school seemed less important (“UnfairDisciplineAtSchool” and “SchoolConnectedness” were the two lowest exponentiated logistic regression coefficients.)

Results and Interpretation
The classification tree offered less predictive power than the past two models (with an AUC of 0.54), but it provided clear insight into which factors most influenced weapon-carrying behavior. The decision tree’s structure made it easy to understand how the model worked, with prediction paths splitting based on the truth-values of variables.
To arrive at the final model, I used an iterative tuning process, systematically testing combinations of parameters like tree depth and complexity to find the best-performing setup. This trial-and-error refinement—core to machine learning—allowed the model to adjust based on feedback from the data, even if its ultimate performance remained modest.

title: Classification Tree
text: Decision tree is a predictive modeling technique that uses a tree-like structure to split data based on feature values. It can be used for both classification and regression tasks. The model uses machine learning to recursively partition the dataset into subsets based on the variable that best separates the data at each step, resulting in a hierarchy of decision rules.

title: Lasso Regression
text:
Lasso regression is a statistical model that combines linear/logistic regression with L1 regularization to perform both variable selection and regularization. The term “Lasso” stands for “Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator.” This method is particularly useful when dealing with datasets that have many predictors, as it helps to:

Reduce overfitting by penalizing large coefficients
Perform automatic feature selection by shrinking some coefficients to exactly zero
Handle multicollinearity by selecting only one variable from a group of highly correlated predictors

In this analysis, I used Lasso regression to predict weapon carrying behavior in schools, demonstrating how this method can help identify the most important predictors while maintaining model interpretability.

title: Random Forest
text: I used a random forest model to predict weapon-carrying behavior in schools. Random forest is a non-parametric ensemble method that builds many decision trees and combines their predictions. Unlike a single decision tree, which is often unstable and prone to overfitting, random forest improves predictive performance by averaging results across many trees.

Results and Interpretation
The random forest model slightly outperformed my previous models in terms of discriminative ability, achieving an AUC of 0.703. It’s interesting to see how different machine learning models perform better/worse than others. The upgrade in predictive power from a singular decision tree (AUC of 0.54) to a random forest (AUC of 0.7) exemplifies the importance of creating multiple models to avoid overfitting and capture more complex relationships. As for the model itself, the model was tuned with a relatively small mtry of 2 and a min_n of 17, which suggests that shallow trees and minimal predictor sampling worked best to avoid overfitting. It’s likely this reflects the high class imbalance and multicollinearity in the dataset—forcing the model to generalize more simply helped improve its generalization to unseen data.

As a conservative estimate, let’s assume there are 5,000 traders who are more trading in higher volume than me (it’s probably higher.) This means there are 5,000 traders who likely have paid more in fees. Again, let’s be conservative and assume the average person in this group pays about $3,000 in fees (I know a few people with higher volume than myself who have paid five-figure amounts in fees, so I’m confident that this is conservative.) That would suggest that Kalshi’s total revenue in 2025 is a much, much higher number, but I digress.

If 5,000 people are generating them 8-figures in fees, then it makes sense that they would coddle, encourage, and care for them as much as possible. However, there’s a reason for this. When I build arbitrages, I tend to build them with “No” orders since “No” orders tend to clear faster. This is because buying the “No” is the same as selling the “Yes”, and people will buy your “Yes” contracts more than the “No” by the aforementioned logic on “Yes” being intuitive.

Now I have something else I’d like to test. I only gamble (casting a singular trade and holding until market resolution) when I believe I have significant edge over the given odds - when I believe a market is mispriced. However, is this true?

Let’s see what my profit looks like in markets where I only did a singular trade.

  filter(!is.na(Ticker)) |>
  group_by(Ticker) |>
  mutate(Trades = n()) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(Trades == 1) |>
  summarize(
    Avg_Profit_Single_Trade = mean(Realized_Profit_Clean)
  ) |>

Average Profit for Gambles

7.03







Since my gambles are (on average) profitable and (supposedly) thought-through, can I still be classified as a degenerate gambler? Yes, yes I can.
Sidenote: There are two caveats to this statistic. 

There are some “gambles” (previously defined as buying a position and holding) that aren’t included in this calculation. This is because I filtered for markets where I only did a single trade. Not every “gamble” is captured this way. For example, I may have bought multiple “gambles” in a market, which would make it register as having had multiple trades. However, I don’t have a way of discerning which multi-trade markets are purely gambling vs. trading, so I went with only the markets where I was 100% sure of being gambles. In other words, all single-trade markets are gambles, but not all gambles are single-trade markets. 
Partly caused by the above phenomenon, I have a mildly low sample size (158). This makes me less certain that I’m profitable with gambles.



Moving on, let’s look at when I have done my best and my worst trading.

 Two new entries: my fifth-largest loss and my fifth-largest profit. That new entry in the profit list (KXUFCFIGHT-25JUN21HILROU) is notable, mainly because the UFC market is a new category I’ve experimented with this month. My trading in June was largely defined by developing consistent, profitable strategy on recurring markets (which will be discussed later) but the UFC market is a complete departure from that trend.
UFC markets are not consistently occurring and they’re extremely inefficient/bizarre. More specifically, they’re bizarre in how they behave relative to other sports markets. How? Well, sports markets tend to be heavily botted. Large trading firms create hyper-efficient algorithms that put forth tens of thousands of shares in a very tight spread around their projected probability. This forces traders (like myself) to try to find profit in that tight margin, meaning higher risk and smaller profit percentage. If you’re not careful in these markets, the firms will take your bids and your money as well. However, the UFC offers a conundrum: how do you calculate the probability of winning for a fighter mid-fight? The short answer is: you can’t. At least not well.
To understand why that is, it’s easier to understand first why firms are able to make such tight spreads on (for example) basketball markets mid-game. This is because:

they have a number of objective, constantly updating, and important variables they can punch into their formula.
the plethora of (impactful) variables creates extremely precise projections.

In the UFC, neither of these conditions are met. While, in basketball, you can look at things like scoring totals, shooting efficiency, fouls to give, and so forth, the UFC offers very few variables. I mean, really, what can you track? The only real answer is a variable like punches landed or times knocked down, but that’s little information to work with. The end result is that firms have little information to create live projections with. Even if they do create spreads, the spreads have to be very wide to account for their projections uncertainty due to the low-information nature of the sport.
Anyway, how does this come back to me? Honestly, I just think this is an interesting phenomenon in the world of sports markets. However, this background gives context as to how I was able to make that much money in a single market. Recall when I previously described how trading firms create tight spreads that stifle traders with their unbeatable efficiency and up-to-date information? Well, the opposite happens in the UFC fights. With little to no botted activity whatsoever, there are large spreads with high liquidity, which births great opportunities to quickly build arbitrages with high volume. That allllllll comes back to me making $136 on a fight that lasted 25 minutes.
It’s important to note, though, that the nature of UFC fights being far and few between means that this is neither a large nor consistent source of profit.

With the null hypothesis for both tests being that my true average (or median) profit is less than or equal to zero - meaning I have no consistent profitability or could even be losing - the small p-values seem to suggest that I’m likely profitable. I mean, 1.770e-07 and 2.040e-13 sure seem smaller than the “p-value < 0.05” standard. But, for better understanding, let’s be clear as to what these tests are doing, what they’re saying, and why they’re good (or bad.)

t-test
The t-test assumes a normal distribution and evaluates whether the mean, based on sample size and variance, is significantly greater than 0. What this final p-value means is, under the assumption that my true average profit is zero or negative, the probability of observing a sample mean this large ($9.71) is 0.0000177%. Now, as promising as this is, I don’t know if I believe that my baseball market profitability distribution is normal. Let’s check:

All in all, it’s about normally distributed enough for me to be confident that the t-test carries some validity and proof of my profitability in baseball markets!


Wilcoxon test
Unlike the t-test, the Wilcoxon test doesn’t assume normality, instead evaluating the median profit by ranking each trade’s direction and magnitude. This makes the Wilcoxon test more universal, but less precise. Still, with this final p-value of 2.040e-13, the probability of observing profits this consistently positive is 0.0000277% under the null hypothesis according to the Wilcoxon test. reverse_chromatic <- c("C", "C#", "D", "Eb", "E", "F", "F#", "G", "Ab", "A", "Bb", "B")

major_roman <- c("I", "#I/♭II", "II", "#II/♭III", "III", "IV", "#IV/♭V", "V", "#V/♭VI", "VI", "#VI/♭VII", "VII")
minor_roman <- c("i", "#i/♭II", "ii°", "#ii°/♭III", "III", "iv", "#iv/♭V", "V", "#V/♭VI", "VI", "#VI/♭VII", "vii°")

is_minor_key <- function(key) {
  str_detect(key, "m") & !str_detect(key, "maj")
}

extract_root <- function(chord) {
  matches <- str_match(chord, "^([A-G][b#]?)")
  matches[,2]
}

convert_chord_to_roman <- function(chord, key) {
  chord <- str_trim(chord)
  if (is.na(chord) || chord == "") return("")

  key_root <- extract_root(key)
  if (is.na(key_root) || !(key_root %in% names(chromatic_scale))) return(chord)

  tonic_val <- chromatic_scale[[key_root]]
  minor_mode <- is_minor_key(key)
  roman_labels <- if (minor_mode) minor_roman else major_roman

  romanize <- function(note, quality = "") {
    if (!(note %in% names(chromatic_scale))) return(paste0(note, quality))
    interval <- (chromatic_scale[[note]] - tonic_val) %% 12
    paste0(roman_labels[interval + 1], quality)
  }

  # 1. Slash chords (e.g., C/G)
  if (str_detect(chord, "/")) {
    parts <- str_split(chord, "/")[[1]]
    if (length(parts) != 2) return(chord)
    main <- str_trim(parts[1])
    bass <- str_trim(parts[2])

    main_root <- extract_root(main)
    bass_root <- extract_root(bass)

    if (is.na(main_root) || is.na(bass_root)) return(chord)

    main_qual <- str_remove(main, main_root)
    main_roman <- romanize(main_root, main_qual)
    bass_roman <- romanize(bass_root)

    return(paste0(main_roman, "/", bass_roman))
  }

  # 2. Substitution chords (e.g., Cmaj7(Am7))
  if (str_detect(chord, "\\(")) {
    matches <- str_match(chord, "^([A-G][b#]?[^\\(]*)\\(([^\\)]+)\\)")
    if (any(is.na(matches))) return(chord)

    outer <- str_trim(matches[, 2])
    inner <- str_trim(matches[, 3])

    outer_root <- extract_root(outer)
    inner_root <- extract_root(inner)

    if (is.na(outer_root) || is.na(inner_root)) return(chord)

    outer_qual <- str_remove(outer, outer_root)
    inner_qual <- str_remove(inner, inner_root)

    outer_roman <- romanize(outer_root, outer_qual)
    inner_roman <- romanize(inner_root, inner_qual)

    return(paste0(outer_roman, "(", inner_roman, ")"))
  }

  # 3. Regular chords
  root <- extract_root(chord)
  if (is.na(root)) return(chord)

  qual <- str_remove(chord, root)
  romanize(root, qual)
}




Bigram Markov Function
In this section, I built a simple generative model using bigrams, which are just pairs of consecutive chords (e.g., I → ii, ii → V). By analyzing every chord progression in the dataset, the function counts how often each chord was followed by another and used those counts to calculate transition probabilities. The generate_sequence() function then uses these probabilities to simulate new progressions—starting from a given chord (like “I”) and sampling each next chord based on the real-world patterns learned from the data.

tokenize_chords <- function(prog) {
  bars <- str_split(prog, "\\|")[[1]]
  chords <- unlist(str_split(bars, ","))
  str_trim(chords[chords != ""])
}

chord_sequences <- CPWK$RomanNumeralProgression %>%
  map(tokenize_chords)

bigrams <- map(chord_sequences, ~ tibble(
  from = head(.x, -1),
  to   = tail(.x, -1)
)) %>% bind_rows()

bigram_counts <- bigrams %>%
  count(from, to, name = "n") %>%
  group_by(from) %>%
  mutate(prob = n / sum(n)) %>%
  ungroup()

generate_sequence <- function(start = "I", max_length = 16) {
  seq <- c(start)
  while (length(seq) < max_length) {
    options <- bigram_counts %>% filter(from == last(seq))
    if (nrow(options) == 0) break
    next_chord <- sample(options$to, size = 1, prob = options$prob)
    seq <- c(seq, next_chord)
  }
  return(seq)
}

It’s alive! I have a lot of thoughts, but let’s focus on the positives:

The chord progressions (for the most part) are theoretically sound! For example, Chord Progression [01] has a great ending. The VI chord into the IIm7-V7 is a good idea, and the IIm7-V7 is perfectly resolved by restarting the chord progression (i.e. going back to the I chord.) There are highs and lows, but you’ll have to trust me when I say that - for the most part - there’s some coherence here. At least more than previous scrapped models.
Basic resolution patterns seem to be followed. Coverting Results Back to Standard Chords
I’m almost done here, but there’s one step left. Musicians don’t play from chord progressions in Roman Numeral form (think back to the Dinah example), I only did that so the model would capture the chord function within the progression. I wrote code to convert the examples back into standard chords (in the key of C). Additionally, I added an extra feature in the results, and wrote code to test if the resulting chord progression exists in the dataset (i.e. is the model overfitted.) extract_roman_base <- function(roman_string, key_mode = "major") {
  roman_list <- if (key_mode == "minor") minor_roman else major_roman
  roman_list <- roman_list[order(nchar(roman_list), decreasing = TRUE)]
  match <- roman_list[str_detect(roman_string, fixed(roman_list))]
  if (length(match) == 0) return(NA)
  match[[1]]
}

convert_roman_prog_to_chords <- function(roman_prog, key = "C") {
  bars <- str_split(roman_prog, "\\|")[[1]]
  tonic_val <- chromatic_scale[[extract_root(key)]]
  is_minor <- is_minor_key(key)
  key_mode <- if (is_minor) "minor" else "major"
  roman_labels <- if (is_minor) minor_roman else major_roman

  real_chords <- lapply(bars, function(bar) {
    chords <- str_split(str_trim(bar), ",")[[1]]

    sapply(chords, function(rc) {
      rc <- str_trim(rc)
      if (rc == "") return("")

      # 1. Slash chords (e.g. Imaj7/III)
      if (str_detect(rc, "/") & !str_detect(rc, "\\(")) {
        parts <- str_split(rc, "/")[[1]]
        main <- str_trim(parts[1])
        bass <- str_trim(parts[2])
        main_label <- extract_roman_base(main, key_mode)
        bass_label <- extract_roman_base(bass, key_mode)
        if (is.na(main_label) | is.na(bass_label)) return("NA/NA")
        main_qual <- str_remove(main, fixed(main_label))
        bass_interval <- match(bass_label, roman_labels) - 1
        main_interval <- match(main_label, roman_labels) - 1
        bass_note <- reverse_chromatic[(tonic_val + bass_interval) %% 12 + 1]
        main_note <- reverse_chromatic[(tonic_val + main_interval) %% 12 + 1]
        return(paste0(main_note, main_qual, "/", bass_note))
      }

      # 2. Substitution chords (e.g. Imaj7(ii7))
      if (str_detect(rc, "\\(")) {
        matches <- str_match(rc, "^([^\\(]+)\\(([^\\)]+)\\)")
        if (any(is.na(matches))) return("NA/NA")
        outer <- str_trim(matches[,2])
        inner <- str_trim(matches[,3])
        outer_label <- extract_roman_base(outer, key_mode)
        inner_label <- extract_roman_base(inner, key_mode)
        if (is.na(outer_label) | is.na(inner_label)) return("NA/NA")
        outer_qual <- str_remove(outer, fixed(outer_label))
        inner_qual <- str_remove(inner, fixed(inner_label))
        outer_interval <- match(outer_label, roman_labels) - 1
        inner_interval <- match(inner_label, roman_labels) - 1
        outer_note <- reverse_chromatic[(tonic_val + outer_interval) %% 12 + 1]
        inner_note <- reverse_chromatic[(tonic_val + inner_interval) %% 12 + 1]
        return(paste0(outer_note, outer_qual, "(", inner_note, inner_qual, ")"))
      }

      # 3. Regular chord
      roman_label <- extract_roman_base(rc, key_mode)
      if (is.na(roman_label)) return("NA/NA")
      qual <- str_remove(rc, fixed(roman_label))
      interval <- match(roman_label, roman_labels) - 1
      note <- reverse_chromatic[(tonic_val + interval) %% 12 + 1]
      paste0(note, qual)
    })
  })

  paste(sapply(real_chords, function(x) paste(x, collapse = ",")), collapse = " | ")
}

chromatic_scale <- c(
  "C"=0, "C#"=1, "Db"=1,
  "D"=2, "D#"=3, "Eb"=3,

# 3. Logic functions
is_minor_key <- function(key) {
  str_detect(key, "m") & !str_detect(key, "maj")
}

extract_root <- function(chord) {
  matches <- str_match(chord, "^([A-G][b#]?)")
  matches[,2]
}

convert_chord_to_roman <- function(chord, key) {
  chord <- str_trim(chord)
  if (is.na(chord) || chord == "") return("")

  key_root <- extract_root(key)
  if (is.na(key_root) || !(key_root %in% names(chromatic_scale))) return(chord)

  tonic_val <- chromatic_scale[[key_root]]
  minor_mode <- is_minor_key(key)
  roman_labels <- if (minor_mode) minor_roman else major_roman

  romanize <- function(note, quality = "") {
    if (!(note %in% names(chromatic_scale))) return(paste0(note, quality))
    interval <- (chromatic_scale[[note]] - tonic_val) %% 12
    paste0(roman_labels[interval + 1], quality)
  }

  # 1. Slash chords (e.g., C/G)
  if (str_detect(chord, "/")) {
    parts <- str_split(chord, "/")[[1]]
    if (length(parts) != 2) return(chord)
    main <- str_trim(parts[1])
    bass <- str_trim(parts[2])

    main_root <- extract_root(main)
    bass_root <- extract_root(bass)

    if (is.na(main_root) || is.na(bass_root)) return(chord)

    main_qual <- str_remove(main, main_root)
    main_roman <- romanize(main_root, main_qual)
    bass_roman <- romanize(bass_root)

    return(paste0(main_roman, "/", bass_roman))
  }

  # 2. Substitution chords (e.g., Cmaj7(Am7))
  if (str_detect(chord, "\\(")) {
    matches <- str_match(chord, "^([A-G][b#]?[^\\(]*)\\(([^\\)]+)\\)")
    if (any(is.na(matches))) return(chord)

    outer <- str_trim(matches[, 2])
    inner <- str_trim(matches[, 3])

    outer_root <- extract_root(outer)
    inner_root <- extract_root(inner)

    if (is.na(outer_root) || is.na(inner_root)) return(chord)

    outer_qual <- str_remove(outer, outer_root)
    inner_qual <- str_remove(inner, inner_root)

    outer_roman <- romanize(outer_root, outer_qual)
    inner_roman <- romanize(inner_root, inner_qual)

    return(paste0(outer_roman, "(", inner_roman, ")"))
  }

  # 3. Regular chords
  root <- extract_root(chord)
  if (is.na(root)) return(chord)

  qual <- str_remove(chord, root)
  romanize(root, qual)
}

# 4. Full progression converter
convert_progression <- function(prog, key) {
  if (is.na(prog) || is.na(key)) return("")
  bars <- str_split(prog, "\\|")[[1]]
  romanized_bars <- lapply(bars, function(bar) {
    chords <- str_split(bar, ",")[[1]]
    roman_chords <- sapply(chords, function(ch) convert_chord_to_roman(str_trim(ch), key))
    paste(roman_chords, collapse = ",")
  })
  paste(romanized_bars, collapse = "|")
}

extract_roman_base <- function(roman_string, key_mode = "major") {
  roman_list <- if (key_mode == "minor") minor_roman else major_roman
  roman_list <- roman_list[order(nchar(roman_list), decreasing = TRUE)]
  match <- roman_list[str_detect(roman_string, fixed(roman_list))]
  if (length(match) == 0) return(NA)
  match[[1]]
}

# Convert Roman numeral string into real chords in given key (default: C)
convert_roman_prog_to_chords <- function(roman_prog, key = "C") {
  bars <- str_split(roman_prog, "\\|")[[1]]
  tonic_val <- chromatic_scale[[extract_root(key)]]
  is_minor <- is_minor_key(key)
  key_mode <- if (is_minor) "minor" else "major"
  roman_labels <- if (is_minor) minor_roman else major_roman

  real_chords <- lapply(bars, function(bar) {
    chords <- str_split(str_trim(bar), ",")[[1]]

    sapply(chords, function(rc) {
      rc <- str_trim(rc)
      if (rc == "") return("")

      # Slash chords (e.g. Imaj7/III)
      if (str_detect(rc, "/") & !str_detect(rc, "\\(")) {
        parts <- str_split(rc, "/")[[1]]
        main <- str_trim(parts[1])
        bass <- str_trim(parts[2])
        main_label <- extract_roman_base(main, key_mode)
        bass_label <- extract_roman_base(bass, key_mode)
        if (is.na(main_label) | is.na(bass_label)) return("NA/NA")
        main_qual <- str_remove(main, fixed(main_label))
        bass_interval <- match(bass_label, roman_labels) - 1
        main_interval <- match(main_label, roman_labels) - 1
        bass_note <- reverse_chromatic[(tonic_val + bass_interval) %% 12 + 1]
        main_note <- reverse_chromatic[(tonic_val + main_interval) %% 12 + 1]
        return(paste0(main_note, main_qual, "/", bass_note))
      }

      # Substitution chords (e.g. Imaj7(ii7))
      if (str_detect(rc, "\\(")) {
        matches <- str_match(rc, "^([^\\(]+)\\(([^\\)]+)\\)")
        if (any(is.na(matches))) return("NA/NA")
        outer <- str_trim(matches[,2])
        inner <- str_trim(matches[,3])
        outer_label <- extract_roman_base(outer, key_mode)
        inner_label <- extract_roman_base(inner, key_mode)
        if (is.na(outer_label) | is.na(inner_label)) return("NA/NA")
        outer_qual <- str_remove(outer, fixed(outer_label))
        inner_qual <- str_remove(inner, fixed(inner_label))
        outer_interval <- match(outer_label, roman_labels) - 1
        inner_interval <- match(inner_label, roman_labels) - 1
        outer_note <- reverse_chromatic[(tonic_val + outer_interval) %% 12 + 1]
        inner_note <- reverse_chromatic[(tonic_val + inner_interval) %% 12 + 1]
        return(paste0(outer_note, outer_qual, "(", inner_note, inner_qual, ")"))
      }

      # Regular chord
      roman_label <- extract_roman_base(rc, key_mode)
      if (is.na(roman_label)) return("NA/NA")
      qual <- str_remove(rc, fixed(roman_label))
      interval <- match(roman_label, roman_labels) - 1
      note <- reverse_chromatic[(tonic_val + interval) %% 12 + 1]
      paste0(note, qual)
    })
  })

  paste(sapply(real_chords, function(x) paste(x, collapse = ",")), collapse = " | ")
}

chromatic_scale <- c(

reverse_chromatic <- c("C", "C#", "D", "Eb", "E", "F", "F#", "G", "Ab", "A", "Bb", "B")

major_roman <- c("I", "#I/♭II", "II", "#II/♭III", "III", "IV", "#IV/♭V", "V", "#V/♭VI", "VI", "#VI/♭VII", "VII")
minor_roman <- c("i", "#i/♭II", "ii°", "#ii°/♭III", "III", "iv", "#iv/♭V", "V", "#V/♭VI", "VI", "#VI/♭VII", "vii°")

is_minor_key <- function(key) {
  str_detect(key, "m") & !str_detect(key, "maj")
}

extract_root <- function(chord) {
  matches <- str_match(chord, "^([A-G][b#]?)")
  matches[,2]
}

convert_chord_to_roman <- function(chord, key) {
  chord <- str_trim(chord)
  if (is.na(chord) || chord == "") return("")

  key_root <- extract_root(key)
  if (is.na(key_root) || !(key_root %in% names(chromatic_scale))) return(chord)

  tonic_val <- chromatic_scale[[key_root]]
  minor_mode <- is_minor_key(key)
  roman_labels <- if (minor_mode) minor_roman else major_roman

  romanize <- function(note, quality = "") {
    if (!(note %in% names(chromatic_scale))) return(paste0(note, quality))
    interval <- (chromatic_scale[[note]] - tonic_val) %% 12
    paste0(roman_labels[interval + 1], quality)
  }

  # 1. Slash chords (e.g., C/G)
  if (str_detect(chord, "/")) {
    parts <- str_split(chord, "/")[[1]]
    if (length(parts) != 2) return(chord)
    main <- str_trim(parts[1])
    bass <- str_trim(parts[2])

    main_root <- extract_root(main)
    bass_root <- extract_root(bass)

    if (is.na(main_root) || is.na(bass_root)) return(chord)

    main_qual <- str_remove(main, main_root)
    main_roman <- romanize(main_root, main_qual)
    bass_roman <- romanize(bass_root)

    return(paste0(main_roman, "/", bass_roman))
  }

  # 2. Substitution chords (e.g., Cmaj7(Am7))
  if (str_detect(chord, "\\(")) {
    matches <- str_match(chord, "^([A-G][b#]?[^\\(]*)\\(([^\\)]+)\\)")
    if (any(is.na(matches))) return(chord)

    outer <- str_trim(matches[, 2])
    inner <- str_trim(matches[, 3])

    outer_root <- extract_root(outer)
    inner_root <- extract_root(inner)

    if (is.na(outer_root) || is.na(inner_root)) return(chord)

    outer_qual <- str_remove(outer, outer_root)
    inner_qual <- str_remove(inner, inner_root)

    outer_roman <- romanize(outer_root, outer_qual)
    inner_roman <- romanize(inner_root, inner_qual)

    return(paste0(outer_roman, "(", inner_roman, ")"))
  }

  # 3. Regular chords
  root <- extract_root(chord)
  if (is.na(root)) return(chord)

  qual <- str_remove(chord, root)
  romanize(root, qual)
}




Overview of Model Fixes for Increased Complexity
Well, in my narrative for the first model, I said I would just focus on the positives. Now is the time to understand the negatives of my previous model, so you can understand the changes I made in the updated model.

Multiple chords within bars

PROBLEM: If you recall, each chord progression in the previous model allotted one chord per bar
(e.g. Sequence 3: C | Dm7 | G7 | C7 | Fmaj7 | Bm7b5 | E7b9 | A7). This made sense for simplicity’s sake, but that’s not how jazz progressions work in reality; often times, there are multiple chord changes within a singular bar. So, I had to figure out a way to impliment that into my model.
FIX: I redesigned the model architecture around full bars rather than individual chords. Instead of treating each chord as an atomic unit, I treated each bar as a block of harmonic context - whether it contains one chord or several. The key insight was to condition transitions not from chord to chord, but from bar to bar, based on the relationship between the last chord of the previous bar and the first chord of the next.
The updated code has the following logic tunnel:

The model starts with a predefined starting chord (e.g., “I”).
It searches the bar metadata for all bars that begin with that chord.
From that filtered set, it selects one bar (using probabilistic frequencies) to serve as the first bar of the sequence.
It then extracts the last chord of that selected bar.
Using the transition table, it finds bars whose first chord transitions well from the previous bar’s last chord.
From those matching bars, it samples the next bar according to the learned transition probabilities.
This process repeats:


Each time, the last chord of the current bar is used to condition the choice of the next bar’s first chord.
Only transitions that preserve chord-to-chord continuity across bar boundaries are considered.

The result is a bar-level sequence, where each measure can contain multiple chords (it’s still possible to only have one chord within a bar), but all transitions are both harmonically valid and empirically grounded in real jazz progressions.

Training the progression on data with the same chord quality

PROBLEM: Another issue that popped up in the previous model was some chords being flat-out weird. Here are some chord changes that the previous model suggested (in my own experimentation) which I found to be odd:

#I/♭II7 → Im6 (Why is the #I resolving to a minor I)
#V/♭VI7 → #VI/♭VIImaj7 (Neither #V or #VI are in a major key)
#IV/♭V07 → Im7/V (Same problem as the above chord change)

In case you haven’t noticed, the problem with these chord changes is that none of them make sense in the context of a major key (which all my progressions are based in). What I realized is that the model was sampling from major as well as minor progressions, which throws off generated progressions. As you can see below, all three of these individual chord changes which I noted as “odd” come from minor progressions in the database.

FIX: I updated the model to only train on progressions that match the mode (major or minor) of the starting chord. That means:

If I set the starting chord to “I”, the model will only train from major-mode chord progressions.
If I set it to “Im”, the model will only train from minor-mode chord progressions.

This ensures that the statistical patterns it learns are harmonically consistent with the type of progression being generated.

Eliminating chord repitition

PROBLEM: Of the many chord changes that can occur in jazz, one of the most common is “resting” on a chord (i.e. repeating the same chord). This typically only occurs for two or three bars, but my model doesn’t know that. Because of the frequency with which “resting” occurs, my model often generates the same chord repeatedly. For example, here are some laughable chord progressions that my previous model generated:

It’s funny but also incredibly stupid.
FIX: I simply hard-coded the model to avoid excessive repetition. Specifically, if the same bar is repeated twice, the model is barred from picking it for a third time and must deviate.

convert_bar_to_chords <- function(bar, key = "C") {
  tonic_val <- chromatic_scale[[extract_root(key)]]
  is_minor <- is_minor_key(key)
  key_mode <- if (is_minor) "minor" else "major"
  roman_labels <- if (is_minor) minor_roman else major_roman

  chords <- str_split(str_trim(bar), ",")[[1]] %>% str_trim()

  real_chords <- sapply(chords, function(rc) {
    if (rc == "") return("")

    # Slash chord
    if (str_detect(rc, "/") & !str_detect(rc, "\\(")) {
      parts <- str_split(rc, "/")[[1]]
      main <- str_trim(parts[1])
      bass <- str_trim(parts[2])
      main_label <- extract_roman_base(main, key_mode)
      bass_label <- extract_roman_base(bass, key_mode)
      if (is.na(main_label) | is.na(bass_label)) return("NA/NA")
      main_qual <- str_remove(main, fixed(main_label))
      bass_interval <- match(bass_label, roman_labels) - 1
      main_interval <- match(main_label, roman_labels) - 1
      bass_note <- reverse_chromatic[(tonic_val + bass_interval) %% 12 + 1]
      main_note <- reverse_chromatic[(tonic_val + main_interval) %% 12 + 1]
      return(paste0(main_note, main_qual, "/", bass_note))
    }

    # Substitution chord
    if (str_detect(rc, "\\(")) {
      matches <- str_match(rc, "^([^\\(]+)\\(([^\\)]+)\\)")
      if (any(is.na(matches))) return("NA/NA")
      outer <- str_trim(matches[,2])
      inner <- str_trim(matches[,3])
      outer_label <- extract_roman_base(outer, key_mode)
      inner_label <- extract_roman_base(inner, key_mode)
      if (is.na(outer_label) | is.na(inner_label)) return("NA/NA")
      outer_qual <- str_remove(outer, fixed(outer_label))
      inner_qual <- str_remove(inner, fixed(inner_label))
      outer_interval <- match(outer_label, roman_labels) - 1
      inner_interval <- match(inner_label, roman_labels) - 1
      outer_note <- reverse_chromatic[(tonic_val + outer_interval) %% 12 + 1]
      inner_note <- reverse_chromatic[(tonic_val + inner_interval) %% 12 + 1]
      return(paste0(outer_note, outer_qual, "(", inner_note, inner_qual, ")"))
    }

    # Regular chord
    roman_label <- extract_roman_base(rc, key_mode)
    if (is.na(roman_label)) return("NA/NA")
    qual <- str_remove(rc, fixed(roman_label))
    interval <- match(roman_label, roman_labels) - 1
    note <- reverse_chromatic[(tonic_val + interval) %% 12 + 1]
    paste0(note, qual)
  })

  paste(real_chords, collapse = ", ")
}

build_probability_tree <- function(start_first_chord = "I", max_depth = 2, top_n = 5) {
  start_bars <- bar_info %>%
    filter(first_chord == start_first_chord) %>%
    pull(bar)
  
  if (length(start_bars) == 0) stop("No starting bars found.")
  start_bar <- sample(start_bars, 1)

  tree_edges <- tibble(from = character(), to = character(), prob = numeric())
  visited <- c()

  expand_node <- function(current_bar, depth) {
    if (depth > max_depth) return()
    current_last <- bar_info$last_chord[bar_info$bar == current_bar]
    if (length(current_last) == 0) return()

    transitions <- transition_probs %>%
      filter(last_chord_from == current_last) %>%
      arrange(desc(prob)) %>%
      slice_head(n = top_n)

    for (i in seq_len(nrow(transitions))) {
      child_bar <- transitions$bar_to[i]
      edge <- tibble(from = current_bar, to = child_bar, prob = transitions$prob[i])
      tree_edges <<- bind_rows(tree_edges, edge)

      if (!(child_bar %in% visited)) {
        visited <<- c(visited, child_bar)
        expand_node(child_bar, depth + 1)
      }
    }
  }

  visited <- c(start_bar)
  expand_node(start_bar, 1)
  list(edges = tree_edges, root = start_bar)
}

title: Project Overview
text:
Background
Now, as much as I’d like to live in a world where everyone had a baseline level of jazz-theory knowledge, that is (sadly) not reality. Therefore, it’s necessary to provide a simple explanation of what a chord progression is and its function in jazz music.
Chord progressions simply are defined as a sequence of chords over a blocked amount of musical time. They are not instructions on what to play specifically, as much as they are describing the harmonic backbone of a musical piece. For example, an overly-simplistic chord progression would be:
\(|\ \text{C}\ |\ \text{Am}\ |\ \text{F}\ |\ \text{G}\ |\). What this means is that, for the four bars of this progression, the first bar is in the key of C, the second in A minor, etc. This is simply just a framework. Jazz musicians then take these progressions and play over them. This means they’re constantly aware of what measure they’re in within the progression, and then improvise their melodies or perform they’re comping (short for “accompanying”, meaning to provide background harmonics to outline the progression) all based on the current key of the progression.
How does this look in jazz? Well, jazz music is typically stored in something called “lead sheets”. A lead sheet condenses a song down to its essential elements: the melody (usually notated in standard notation) and the chord progression (written above the staff). This is all a jazz musician needs to interpret and perform a tune — the rest is up to personal style and improvisation. For example, look at the below lead sheet for a personal favorite standard of mine, Dinah.











As you can see above, lead sheets are noticingly sparse, but any half-decent jazz combo should be able to use the progression within the lead sheet to immediately understand how to provide harmonies, the context in which to solo, and the direction of the tune. That’s the power of the jazz chord progression; the minimal instructions and shared outline create entire songs full of natural interaction and improvisation.

In case you can’t tell by now, a key part of being a jazz musician is being able to pick up and play around progressions on the fly. One such way I learned to practice this ability, is through something called “The Game of Chords”.
In it, each card represents a single bar of harmony, and the properties of the card determine the type of chord in that bar. Specifically:
The rank (Ace through 7) determines the scale degree, or the chord’s root relative to a key. For example:

1 (Ace) = I
2 = II
3 = III
4 = IV
etc.

The suit tells you the quality of the chord, i.e., whether it’s major, minor, dominant, or diminished:

Hearts = major (e.g., IV, I)
Spades = minor (e.g., ii, vi)
Diamonds = dominant seventh (e.g., V7)
Clubs = diminished or half-diminished

So for example, the 5 of Diamonds would represent a V7 chord.
You deal yourself some amount of cards (typically 4 or 8) and then are forced to improvise on the spot over the drawn chord progression. It’s a great exercise, but I noticed a problem: without any logic and only pure randomness, you often get chord progressions with no cohesion. Frankly, most chord progressions from this game are atonal, dissonant, and most importantly unrealistic. It’s good to have the experience of dealing with challenging chord progressions on the fly, but they’re often unsatisfying and difficult to learn from as they’re so dissimilar from real-world progressions.
That’s the inspiration for this project: by blending jazz intuition with probabilistic modeling, I hope to build a model that generates chord progressions with enough structure to feel intentional, yet enough variation to remain unique and useful for practicing.

Surprisingly enough, one of the most challenging parts of this project was to create a dataset for the model. There is no easily accesible dataset with jazz chord progressions, at least one that was correctly formatted for an LLM. To start, I was able to find a Github repository with almost 1,000 progressions. I took it upon myself to download the JSON file, filter the progressions, and mutate the dataset to be functional for the model.

Firstly, to ensure consistency in the training data, I filtered for progressions in 4/4 time and exactly 8 bars. This standardization helps the jazz progression LLM learn from structurally comparable examples.
For example, the bar \(|\ \text{Am}\ , \text{D7}\ |\) implies a different rhythm in 3/4 time as opposed to 4/4. This showcases the importance of normalizing time signature. As for the 8 bars, this length is a common phrase structure in jazz, especially within A sections. Limiting to 8-bar segments ensures the model learns patterns that fit within a musically coherent and widely used harmonic unit, improving the relevance and musicality of generated progressions.
Lastly, as some songs were double-counted in the repository, I ensured each song only appeared once in the dataset.

count_bars <- function(chord_string) {
  bars <- str_split(chord_string, "\\|")[[1]]
  sum(str_trim(bars) != "")

a_sections_8bars_4 <- map_df(jazz_data, function(tune) {
  title <- tune$Title
  time_sig <- tune$TimeSignature
  sections <- tune$Sections

  if (is.null(time_sig) || time_sig != "4/4") return(NULL)

  map_df(sections, function(section) {
    if (!is.null(section$Label) && section$Label == "A") {
      chords <- section$MainSegment$Chords
      if (!is.null(chords) && count_bars(chords) == 8) {
        tibble(
          Title = title,
          ChordProgression = chords
        )
      } else {

      }
    } else {

    }
  })

Then came the most challenging part. The most important step in preparing this dataset for the LLM was converting the progression from standard chord symbols into Roman numeral notation. While chords like “Cmaj7” or “Am7” carry harmonic meaning, their function within the progression is key-dependent. For example, Cmaj7 serves as the “I chord” in the key of C, the “home base” chord. It provides resolution and stability. However, in the key of F, Cmaj7 serves as the “V chord”, which begs to be resolved back to the “I chord” (in this case F.) In that case, it is the antithesis of resolution, providing tension instead. This distinction is critical for the LLM because it allows the model to focus on harmonic roles rather than absolute pitches.
I built a set of helper functions and mappings to identify enharmonic equivalents and properly assign chords to their relative Roman numerals based on key context. This included support for complex chord types like slash chords (e.g., C/E) and substitutions (e.g., Cmaj7(Am7)), which are common in jazz but easy to mishandle in automated systems.
Other than that, there were some small formatting issues that I fixed within in the raw chord strings (e.g. removing redundant commas, trimming whitespace, and fixing formatting issues like misplaced commas before barlines or parentheses.) This was necessary to avoid parsing errors later on (as I discovered in my hours of coding errors.)

major_roman <- c("I", "#I/♭II", "II", "#II/♭III", "III", "IV", "#IV/♭V", "V", "#V/♭VI", "VI", "#VI/♭VII", "VII")
minor_roman <- c("i", "#i/♭II", "ii°", "#ii°/♭III", "III", "iv", "#iv/♭V", "V", "#V/♭VI", "VI", "#VI/♭VII", "vii°")

is_minor_key <- function(key) {
  str_detect(key, "m") & !str_detect(key, "maj")
}

extract_root <- function(chord) {
  matches <- str_match(chord, "^([A-G][b#]?)")
  matches[,2]
}

convert_chord_to_roman <- function(chord, key) {
  chord <- str_trim(chord)
  if (is.na(chord) || chord == "") return("")

  key_root <- extract_root(key)
  if (is.na(key_root) || !(key_root %in% names(chromatic_scale))) return(chord)

  tonic_val <- chromatic_scale[[key_root]]
  minor_mode <- is_minor_key(key)
  roman_labels <- if (minor_mode) minor_roman else major_roman

  romanize <- function(note, quality = "") {
    if (!(note %in% names(chromatic_scale))) return(paste0(note, quality))
    interval <- (chromatic_scale[[note]] - tonic_val) %% 12
    paste0(roman_labels[interval + 1], quality)
  }

  # 1. Slash chords (e.g., C/G)
  if (str_detect(chord, "/")) {
    parts <- str_split(chord, "/")[[1]]
    if (length(parts) != 2) return(chord)
    main <- str_trim(parts[1])
    bass <- str_trim(parts[2])

    main_root <- extract_root(main)
    bass_root <- extract_root(bass)

    if (is.na(main_root) || is.na(bass_root)) return(chord)

    main_qual <- str_remove(main, main_root)
    main_roman <- romanize(main_root, main_qual)
    bass_roman <- romanize(bass_root)

    return(paste0(main_roman, "/", bass_roman))
  }

  # 2. Substitution chords (e.g., Cmaj7(Am7))

Firstly, to ensure consistency in the training data, I filtered for progressions in 4/4 time and exactly 8 bars. This standardization helps the jazz progression LLM learn from structurally comparable examples.
For example, the bar \(|\ \text{Am}\ , \text{D7}\ |\) implies a different rhythm in 3/4 time as opposed to 4/4. This showcases the importance of normalizing time signature. As for the 8 bars, this length is a common phrase structure in jazz, especially within A sections. Limiting to 8-bar segments ensures the model learns patterns that fit within a musically coherent and widely used harmonic unit, improving the relevance and musicality of generated progressions.
Lastly, as some songs were double-counted in the repository, I ensured each song only appeared once in the dataset.

Then came the most challenging part. The most important step in preparing this dataset for the LLM was converting the progression from standard chord symbols into Roman numeral notation. While chords like “Cmaj7” or “Am7” carry harmonic meaning, their function within the progression is key-dependent. For example, Cmaj7 serves as the “I chord” in the key of C, the “home base” chord. It provides resolution and stability. However, in the key of F, Cmaj7 serves as the “V chord”, which begs to be resolved back to the “I chord” (in this case F.) In that case, it is the antithesis of resolution, providing tension instead. This distinction is critical for the LLM because it allows the model to focus on harmonic roles rather than absolute pitches.
I built a set of helper functions and mappings to identify enharmonic equivalents and properly assign chords to their relative Roman numerals based on key context. This included support for complex chord types like slash chords (e.g., C/E) and substitutions (e.g., Cmaj7(Am7)), which are common in jazz but easy to mishandle in automated systems.
Other than that, there were some small formatting issues that I fixed within in the raw chord strings (e.g. removing redundant commas, trimming whitespace, and fixing formatting issues like misplaced commas before barlines or parentheses.) This was necessary to avoid parsing errors later on (as I discovered in my hours of coding errors.)

title: Project Overview
section: Optional Background Explenation of Jazz Chord Progressions
text:
Optional Background Explenation of Jazz Chord Progressions
Now, as much as I’d like to live in a world where everyone had a baseline level of jazz-theory knowledge, that is (sadly) not reality. Therefore, it’s necessary to provide a simple explanation of what a chord progression is and its function in jazz music.
Chord progressions simply are defined as a sequence of chords over a blocked amount of musical time. They are not instructions on what to play specifically, as much as they are describing the harmonic backbone of a musical piece. For example, an overly-simplistic chord progression would be:
\(|\ \text{C}\ |\ \text{Am}\ |\ \text{F}\ |\ \text{G}\ |\). What this means is that, for the four bars of this progression, the first bar is in the key of C, the second in A minor, etc. This is simply just a framework. Jazz musicians then take these progressions and play over them. This means they’re constantly aware of what measure they’re in within the progression, and then improvise their melodies or perform they’re comping (short for “accompanying”, meaning to provide background harmonics to outline the progression) all based on the current key of the progression.
How does this look in jazz? Well, jazz music is typically stored in something called “lead sheets”. A lead sheet condenses a song down to its essential elements: the melody (usually notated in standard notation) and the chord progression (written above the staff). This is all a jazz musician needs to interpret and perform a tune — the rest is up to personal style and improvisation. For example, look at the below lead sheet for a personal favorite standard of mine, Dinah.











As you can see above, lead sheets are noticingly sparse, but any half-decent jazz combo should be able to use the progression within the lead sheet to immediately understand how to provide harmonies, the context in which to solo, and the direction of the tune. That’s the power of the jazz chord progression; the minimal instructions and shared outline create entire songs full of natural interaction and improvisation.

In case you can’t tell by now, a key part of being a jazz musician is being able to pick up and play around progressions on the fly. One such way I learned to practice this ability, is through something called “The Game of Chords”.
In it, each card represents a single bar of harmony, and the properties of the card determine the type of chord in that bar. Specifically:
The rank (Ace through 7) determines the scale degree, or the chord’s root relative to a key. For example:

1 (Ace) = I
2 = II
3 = III
4 = IV
etc.

The suit tells you the quality of the chord, i.e., whether it’s major, minor, dominant, or diminished:

Hearts = major (e.g., IV, I)
Spades = minor (e.g., ii, vi)
Diamonds = dominant seventh (e.g., V7)
Clubs = diminished or half-diminished

So for example, the 5 of Diamonds would represent a V7 chord.
You deal yourself some amount of cards (typically 4 or 8) and then are forced to improvise on the spot over the drawn chord progression. It’s a great exercise, but I noticed a problem: without any logic and only pure randomness, you often get chord progressions with no cohesion. Frankly, most chord progressions from this game are atonal, dissonant, and most importantly unrealistic. It’s good to have the experience of dealing with challenging chord progressions on the fly, but they’re often unsatisfying and difficult to learn from as they’re so dissimilar from real-world progressions.
That’s the inspiration for this project: by blending jazz intuition with probabilistic modeling, I hope to build a model that generates chord progressions with enough structure to feel intentional, yet enough variation to remain unique and useful for practicing.

Examples!
One fundamental flaw in presenting this project is that, for 99% of people, there’s no way to tell if the jazz progressions that my program is generating are good. I’ve been consistently making tweaks based on my ability to recognize flaws in the progressions, but it’s not clear to the average reader how much more coherent the progressions are getting just by looking at them.

Baseball Markets
Let there be some arbitrary moments in a baseball game A, B, C, D, E, and F. These could be things like “The game is tied”, “Bases are loaded”, “Rain delay”, etc. Again, this being arbitrary, let’s say my previous strategy was to trade at moments A, C, E, and F.

With strong return totals over time using this strategy, it’s easy to incorrectly assume that each individual moment is profitable. Some moments might have made large amounts of money while others could have been break-even or outright losses. Looking at the final number obscures that nuance. There are many such ways this can be true. For example, let’s say trading at C lost me $500 while A made me $500, E made me $700, and F made me $1,300. The overall P/L is $2,000, which can lead to me incorrectly believing that I’ve chosen the correct moments to trade at. However, C seems to be losing me money.
There’s even more nuance to be had; isolated profit from trading at a moment does not mean true long-term profitability from said moment. For example, let’s say A has an extreme but rare downside risk. Something where A resolves to +$50 P/L 95% of the time, but resolves to -$1,000 P/L 5% of the time (this is way oversimplified and trades don’t simply “resolve” like this, but it’s for the sake of an argument.) The EV of trading at A is -$2.5, but if I only trade at moment A 10 times in a month, you will most likely not see a single one of those losses (~59%):

\[
P(\text{at least one loss}) = 1 - 0.95^{10} \approx 1 - 0.5987 = 0.4013
\]
Again, this would make it easy to incorrectly conclude that A is profitable, even if it’s made money over a period of time.
These are the types of situations I found myself dealing with while optimizing my trading strategy for the baseball markets; using intuitive reasoning to eliminate certain moments from my trading strategy that I found unprofitable/high risk. compute_baseball_stats <- function(df, month_num) {
  df %>%
    filter(Category == "Baseball", month(Created_Parsed) == month_num) %>%
    group_by(Ticker) %>%
    summarise(
      Profit    = sum(Realized_Profit_Clean, na.rm = TRUE),
      Contracts = sum(Contracts, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    summarise(
      Markets         = n(),
      Total_Contracts = sum(Contracts, na.rm = TRUE),
      Total_Profit    = sum(Profit, na.rm = TRUE),
      Home_Runs       = sum(Profit >= 100, na.rm = TRUE),
      ProfitPerCtr    = ifelse(sum(Contracts, na.rm = TRUE) > 0,
                               sum(Profit, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(Contracts, na.rm = TRUE), NA_real_)
    )
}

`%||%` <- function(x, y) if (is.null(x) || is.na(x)) y else x

  ProfitPerCtr    <- stats$ProfitPerCtr %||% NA_real_

  fmt_ppc  <- if (is.na(ProfitPerCtr)) "—" else dollar(ProfitPerCtr, accuracy = 0.0001)
  fmt_prof <- dollar(Total_Profit)
  fmt_ctr  <- comma(Total_Contracts)

  # wider canvas + separate label/value columns (no divider line)
  xmin <- 0; xmax <- 7.2; ymin <- 0; ymax <- 9

  value_x <- 6.6

  ggplot() +

    geom_rect(aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = 7.6, ymax = 9),
              fill = primary, color = primary) +
    geom_rect(aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = 7.2, ymax = 7.6),

    annotate("text", x = label_x, y = 5.6, label = "G (Markets):",
             hjust = 0, color = "gray30", fontface = "bold", size = 3.6) +
    annotate("text", x = label_x, y = 5.0, label = "AB (Contracts):",
             hjust = 0, color = "gray30", fontface = "bold", size = 3.6) +
    annotate("text", x = label_x, y = 4.4, label = "AVG ($ / Contract):",
             hjust = 0, color = "gray30", fontface = "bold", size = 3.6) +
    annotate("text", x = label_x, y = 3.8, label = "HR (≥ $100 Profit Mkts):",
             hjust = 0, color = "gray30", fontface = "bold", size = 3.6) +
    annotate("text", x = label_x, y = 3.2, label = "Total Profit:",
             hjust = 0, color = "gray30", fontface = "bold", size = 3.6) +

    annotate("text", x = value_x, y = 5.6, label = Markets,
             hjust = 1, color = "black", size = 4.0) +
    annotate("text", x = value_x, y = 5.0, label = fmt_ctr,
             hjust = 1, color = "black", size = 4.0) +
    annotate("text", x = value_x, y = 4.4, label = fmt_ppc,
             hjust = 1, color = accent, fontface = "bold", size = 4.0) +
    annotate("text", x = value_x, y = 3.8, label = Home_Runs,
             hjust = 1, color = "black", size = 4.0) +
    annotate("text", x = value_x, y = 3.2, label = fmt_prof,
             hjust = 1, color = primary, fontface = "bold", size = 4.0) +

    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(xmin, xmax), ylim = c(ymin, ymax), expand = FALSE) +
    theme_void()
}

title: Kalshi Analysis 2025 (Updated July)
text:
Highs and Lows (Markets and Days)
Still, my best month doesn’t mean a flawless month. Let’s overview the highs and lows of July. In the below calendar, you can hover over each date to see the overall profit, the best market, and the worst market on the day. Notably, as part of increased volume and profitability, comes higher numbers in both directions. Note that most days now involve triple-digit profit, but there are also multiple days with a triple-digit deficit.


Show code
july_df <- Kalshi25July_arb %>%
  mutate(Date = as.Date(Created_Parsed)) %>%
  filter(month(Date) == 7)

yr <- unique(year(july_df$Date))
yr <- if (length(yr) == 1) yr else 2025

first_day <- as.Date(sprintf("%d-07-01", yr))
last_day  <- ceiling_date(first_day, "month") - days(1)
all_days  <- tibble(Date = seq(first_day, last_day, by = "day"))

# Daily profit (fill missing days with 0)
daily <- july_df %>%
  group_by(Date) %>%
  summarise(Daily_Profit = sum(Realized_Profit_Clean, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  right_join(all_days, by = "Date") %>%
  mutate(
    Daily_Profit = replace_na(Daily_Profit, 0),
    DayNum = day(Date),
    WeekdayF = factor(
      wday(Date, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE, week_start = 1),
      levels = c("Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun")  # Sunday last
    ),
    offset  = wday(first_day, week_start = 1) - 1,
    WeekRow = ((DayNum - 1 + offset) %/% 7) + 1
  )

# Best & worst market per day (Ticker-level) — do these outside summarise()
by_ticker <- july_df %>%
  group_by(Date, Ticker) %>%
  summarise(PnL = sum(Realized_Profit_Clean, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

best <- by_ticker %>%
  group_by(Date) %>%
  slice_max(order_by = PnL, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  transmute(Date, Best_Ticker = Ticker, Best_PnL = PnL)

worst <- by_ticker %>%
  group_by(Date) %>%
  slice_min(order_by = PnL, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  transmute(Date, Worst_Ticker = Ticker, Worst_PnL = PnL)

plot_df <- daily %>%
  left_join(best,  by = "Date") %>%
  left_join(worst, by = "Date") %>%
  mutate(
    hover = paste0(
      format(Date, "%a, %b %d, %Y"), "<br>",
      "Profit: ", dollar(Daily_Profit), "<br>",
      "Best: ", ifelse(is.na(Best_Ticker), "—", Best_Ticker),
      ifelse(is.na(Best_PnL), "", paste0(" (", dollar(Best_PnL), ")")), "<br>",
      "Worst: ", ifelse(is.na(Worst_Ticker), "—", Worst_Ticker),
      ifelse(is.na(Worst_PnL), "", paste0(" (", dollar(Worst_PnL), ")"))
    )
  )

# ----- Calendar-style heatmap (no week-of-month label) -----
p <- ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = WeekdayF, y = WeekRow, fill = Daily_Profit, text = hover)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.8, width = 0.95, height = 0.9) +
  geom_text(aes(label = DayNum), size = 3.8, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_y_reverse(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.02))) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(
    colors = c("#ff4e50", "#ffffff", "#3cb371"),                  # red → white → green
    values = scales::rescale(c(-500, 0, 500)),                    # where those colors sit
    limits = c(-500, 500),                                        # same as before
    oob = scales::squish,
    labels = scales::dollar_format(),
    name = "Profit"
  ) +
  labs(title = "July Profit Calendar", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, face = "bold", size = 16),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
    axis.text.x = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text") %>%
  layout(legend = list(title = list(text = "Profit (USD)")))






 Something like this is important, because the bigger picture is hard to forget. I have to be OK with these days where I lose $100 (6th and 13th) because the larger calendar is mostly green. It’s part of the risk and variance of trading.
